threat_addresses_requirement.rationale: Risk management for high-risk AI systems must address foreseeable misuse, including manipulation through input channels; indirect prompt injection is a foreseeable manipulation vector

Where automated decisions can cause significant harm, human oversight is required; prompt injection is a primary mechanism by which oversight is bypassed because the agent appears to be operating normally

Cybersecurity requirements for high-risk AI systems explicitly include resilience to attempts by unauthorized third parties to alter the system's use, outputs, or performance; indirect prompt injection is exactly this pattern
Includes policies on the security of network and information systems and incident handling; agent runtimes processing variable-trust content are in scope
Operational resilience requirements applicable to financial entities, including resilience of ICT systems to manipulation through tool-output channels
Agent actions taken under prompt injection may constitute unauthorized automated processing affecting data subjects
Appropriate technical measures including resilience to manipulation are required; isolation of tool-output content from authoritative instructions is such a technical measure
Where automated decisions can cause significant harm, human oversight is required; agents acting outside the user's authorization are operating without the oversight the regulation assumes

Cybersecurity requirements for high-risk AI systems include resilience to unauthorized use; structural authorization confusion is a form of unauthorized use even when no traditional control is bypassed
Includes access control policies and asset management; broad-authority agents are critical assets requiring proportionate controls
Operational resilience and ICT risk management requirements applicable to financial entities, including identity and access management

threat_addresses_requirement.article_or_section: Art. 9 (Identification and classification of ICT supported business functions)
threat_addresses_requirement.rationale: Agents serving multiple business functions across tenants or units must be classified and risk-assessed accordingly
Personal data must be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security; cross-user or cross-tenant data exposure via agent deputy patterns violates this principle
Agent actions taken outside the data subject's authorization context may constitute unauthorized automated processing

threat_addresses_requirement.article_or_section: Art. 25 (Data protection by design and by default)
threat_addresses_requirement.rationale: Agents that retrieve more data than the user is authorized for, even if filtered before output, may fail the data minimization requirement
Appropriate technical measures including pseudonymization and access control are required; broad-authority agents bypassing per-user access control fail this standard
Composed agent actions are a risk class that risk management must explicitly address
Composition that exceeds individual review thresholds defeats the oversight model
Operational resilience requires controls on agent action composition for financial entities
Aggregating individual data points into composites can violate minimization even when each retrieval is permitted
Design must consider composed effects, not only individual operations
Resilience to unauthorized data exposure
Personal data must be protected against unauthorized disclosure
Technical and organizational measures including encryption and access control
Confidentiality of information processed by ICT systems
Includes incident handling and confidentiality protections
Logging requirements for high-risk AI systems
Information about how the AI system operates
Oversight requires understanding of what the system did and why
Reporting requires the ability to reconstruct events
Controllers must be able to demonstrate compliance
Data subjects' rights to explanation depend on auditable decision provenance
Includes logging and incident handling
Data quality and integrity for AI systems
Resilience to adversarial manipulation
Personal data must be accurate; poisoned profiles violate this
Erasure is more complex when data has influenced model behavior or vector embeddings
Integrity of information systems
Multi-agent chains amplify the oversight challenge
Resilience requirements apply to the full system, including inter-agent boundaries
When sub-agents integrate third-party services, third-party risk management applies
Accountability through delegation chains requires audit traceability
Includes supply chain security relevant to multi-agent dependencies
Resilience to manipulation of system output
Technical and organizational measures
Operational resilience including output integrity
Where output exploitation results in unauthorized data access or processing
Goal drift is a risk class requiring management
Oversight is the primary mitigation when technical controls cannot fully prevent goal drift
Stability under varied inputs and contexts
Processing must be for specified purposes; goal drift can violate this
Goal drift often correlates with retrieving more data than necessary
Design must consider goal drift, not only intended use
System must operate reliably without resource exhaustion
Operational resilience including capacity management
Availability and resilience

control_mitigates_threat.rationale: Foundational defense against indirect prompt injection: the structural distinction between content and instruction is what prevents tool-output injections from being elevated to authoritative instruction
Verification at action boundaries prevents injected instructions from triggering consequential actions without review

Identity and authorization context propagation: limits blast radius by ensuring injected instructions cannot exceed the originating user's authorization, even when they successfully manipulate the agent's reasoning
End-to-end audit and accountability: enables post-incident attribution, forensic analysis, and detection of injection-driven actions through reasoning provenance

Identity and authorization context propagation: consolidates user-context propagation, on-behalf-of authorization, tenant boundary enforcement, delegation-context preservation, and per-user authorization scoping. Addresses the structural cause of the deputy problem
Authorization-aware output filtering: even when an agent retrieves data using broader authorization, output to the user is filtered to what the user is independently authorized to see
End-to-end audit and accountability: every agent action must be traceable to the originating user, the agent involved, the delegation chain, and the authorization basis
Provides a fallback when CTL-001 cannot fully scope authorization; high-impact actions get explicit verification regardless of authorization model
Composition tracking and verification at composed-action thresholds is the core defense against tool-chain abuse
End-to-end audit and accountability: enables review of action chains and detection of patterns of legitimate-but-composed harm
Identity and authorization context propagation: constrains the user authority that any chain can leverage
Authorization-aware output filtering: ensures the filtering boundary is the user authorization rather than the channel
Identity and authorization context propagation: per-user scoping at retrieval limits what can be exfiltrated
End-to-end audit and accountability: data-flow audit enables detection of legitimate-channel exfiltration
End-to-end audit and accountability: the control is directly designed to address audit and provenance failure
Identity and authorization context propagation: user attribution in audit records requires context propagation through the agent stack
Tool-output and context provenance: provenance is the input to meaningful audit
Extending provenance to persisted state addresses memory-vector poisoning patterns by preventing persisted content from being treated as authoritative on retrieval
End-to-end audit and accountability: enables forensic review when poisoning is suspected
Action verification at high-impact boundaries: provides a checkpoint when retrieved memory influences high-impact decisions
Identity and authorization context propagation: ensures user context is preserved through the delegation chain
Tool-output and context provenance: tagging sub-agent outputs as content rather than instruction
Action verification at high-impact boundaries: requires verification at the primary agent before acting on sub-agent outputs in high-stakes contexts
End-to-end audit and accountability: enables traceability across the delegation chain
Verification before agent output triggers downstream execution prevents output-injection harm
Provenance tagging helps downstream systems treat agent output appropriately, reducing the risk that consuming systems interpret agent output as instruction
Authorization-aware output filtering: addresses content authorization; less direct on syntactic exploits in output structure
Verification provides a checkpoint where the agent's stated action exceeds expected scope, surfacing context-driven goal drift
End-to-end audit and accountability: enables review of how the agent interpreted its goal
Provenance helps trace which context elements influenced agent reasoning, supporting detection and review of context-driven goal drift
Cumulative resource consumption is itself a high-impact pattern that verification can catch
End-to-end audit and accountability: enables review of loop patterns
Identity and authorization context propagation: limits which user contexts can cause uncontrolled loops

threat_related_to_threat.relationship: Common amplifier: prompt injection becomes more dangerous when combined with broad agent authorization. AGT-001 is the input mechanism; AGT-002 is the structural condition that makes the input mechanism harmful
Prompt injection often drives the chain composition; the injected instruction can direct the agent through a sequence of legitimately authorized tool calls
Persisted content can be the vehicle for injection across sessions; injection that persists to memory becomes a long-term influence on agent behavior
Injection received from one source can be reflected into output that injects another consuming system; AGT-001 is content entering the agent, AGT-008 is content leaving the agent
Prompt injection is one mechanism by which goal subversion occurs, but goal subversion can also occur without explicit injection
Common attack vector that exploits AGT-002; AGT-001 is the input mechanism, AGT-002 is the structural condition
AGT-003 (tool-chain abuse) often depends on the agent having broader authorization than the user, which is AGT-002
One consequence of AGT-002 is that audit trails do not cleanly attribute actions to originating users; AGT-005 compounds AGT-002
The delegation-ambiguity sub-pattern within AGT-002 connects directly to AGT-007 when the delegated entity is another agent rather than a tool
Tool-chain abuse often depends on the agent having broader authorization than the user, which is AGT-002
Prompt injection often drives the chain composition; the injected instruction directs the agent through legitimately authorized tool calls
Authorization confusion is often the precondition that allows the agent to retrieve more than the user is authorized to see
Persistence into memory or vector stores is a sub-pattern of AGT-004 that carries the AGT-006 long-lived exposure characteristic
Authorization confusion compounds audit failure: when the agent acts beyond user scope, the audit trail's gap is also an accountability gap
Detection of injection-driven action depends on the kind of provenance AGT-005 highlights
Persisted content can be the vehicle for injection across sessions; AGT-001 plus persistence becomes AGT-006
Detection of memory poisoning depends on the persistence boundary provenance described in AGT-005
The delegation-ambiguity sub-pattern within AGT-002 connects directly to AGT-007 when the delegated entity is another agent rather than a tool
Output-as-instruction is the inter-agent variant of indirect prompt injection: one agent's output becomes another agent's adversarial input
Inverse direction: AGT-001 is content entering the agent, AGT-008 is content leaving the agent. The two together cover the cross-system trust boundaries
Output to another agent in a multi-agent system is the AGT-007 dimension of AGT-008
Prompt injection is one mechanism by which goal subversion occurs, but goal subversion can also occur without explicit injection
Memory poisoning can be a pathway for goal subversion that persists across sessions
Goal subversion can drive an agent into loops when its interpretation of the task does not converge
Loop detection often depends on the kind of cumulative-action audit AGT-005 highlights
